atv2-b4-p1.transcript: Vaissalu's drawings, set beside the stones that still stand. He drew some forty memorials in the seventeen nineties; nine of those stones survive. The comparison isn't flattering. The letterforms he gives are wrong in the same places an earlier antiquarian, Rennik, had gone wrong — same bind-runes, same swallowed vowel. He was copying Rennik's sketchbook, not the stone. Two things he's innocent of, mind: where a stone had flaked, he leaves a gap, honestly blank; and his churchyard attributions hold up wherever we can test them. How did I come to this? The parsonage at Kolgama. I catalogued its library as a student, one wet summer, and there was Rennik's sketchbook. That's the whole connection — no squeezes have ever come out of that house, the glebe wall there is nineteenth-century brick, and Kolgama's own pastors kept none of the visitation books that first mention the stones. The dating quarrel now. Hallik dates the group later than the years carved on it. I'd narrow that. One carver, the Ansu master, worked late, and his pieces colour how the rest get read; I would not extend that to the group. The formulas are common regional ones, older than any printed model I know, and the stone there weathers fast, so I don't rest a case on weathering. Twenty-odd stones are unlocated. We won't print a text nobody has seen on the stone, and they stay in the corpus volume, marked missing. A handlist goes to the county museums; some may sit unrecognized in a storeroom. The radio appeal was tried upriver and turned up little but field boulders.

explanations.q1: Set against the surviving stones, Vaissalu's letterforms go wrong in exactly the places an earlier antiquarian, Rennik, had gone wrong — he was working from Rennik's sketchbook rather than from the stone.
explanations.q2: Kolgama comes up as a personal aside: the professor catalogued the parsonage library as a student and found Rennik's sketchbook there, which is how he came to the material.
explanations.q3: He does not accept the late-carving argument for the group; he narrows it to one carver, the Ansu master, whose late pieces have coloured how the rest are read.
explanations.q4: For the unlocated stones the plan is a handlist to the county museums, on the chance some are sitting unrecognized in a storeroom.

q1.1: He supplied nothing on the damaged surfaces — where a stone had flaked, "he leaves a gap", honestly blank.
q1.3: The placings are not the problem: "his churchyard attributions hold up" wherever they can be tested.

q2.0: No squeezes came from the parsonage at all — "no squeezes have ever come out" of that house.
q2.1: There is no reused stone in the wall: "the glebe wall there is nineteenth-century brick".
q2.2: The visitation books were not kept there — "Kolgama's own pastors kept none" of them.

q3.0: He refuses the group-wide version outright: "I would not extend that to the group".
q3.1: The formula argument is denied — the memorial formulas are "older than any printed model" he knows.
q3.2: He does not argue from weathering, and says why: "the stone there weathers fast".

q4.2: They are not being separated off: "they stay in the corpus volume", marked missing.
q4.3: The broadcast route has been tried and failed — it "turned up little but field boulders".

atv2-b4-p2.transcript: The nineteen-oh-seven earthquake, then, and what re-reading the old sheets does to it. Start with the logbook from the Luhemaa station. It is a weather book as much as an instrument book, and that is why it earned its keep. A low background rumble sits on the Luhemaa traces that autumn, and the daily wind and sea entries let us set storm surf aside as its source — the rumble is loudest on flat, still days. The observer's felt account went to a newspaper the same week; the logbook closes in the same year the official history gives; and the crate surfaced through a museum's accession list, not through anything in the logbook. Tammik has argued for two ruptures minutes apart, and Oks thinks the magnitude drops once you model those old instruments. Neither holds: the trace shows one rupture, and the magnitude barely moves. The source sits under the coastal parish the catalogues name. What changes is the damage — the river towns stand on soft alluvium, and that, more than the size of the shock, drew the map of ruin. The sheets survive nearly complete. Hardly a sheet is missing from the years the network changed hands, the years before nineteen fifteen are as thickly covered as any, and each sheet carries its station's stamp. The trouble is framing: someone trimmed the margins off for display, and the time marks went with them. Kolmsaare? I am persuaded. The aftershocks sit along its mapped trend. The northern structure fits the uplift no better, these are not scattered shocks in healed crust, and the Kolmsaare structure is young.

explanations.q1: The Luhemaa logbook is a weather book as well as an instrument book, and its daily wind and sea entries let the team set storm surf aside as the source of the background rumble on the traces.
explanations.q2: His central claim is about damage rather than size: the river towns stand on soft alluvium, and the ground conditions there, more than the shock itself, drew the map of ruin.
explanations.q3: The sheets survive nearly complete; what was lost is the trimmed margins, taken off for framing, and the time marks went with them.
explanations.q4: He is persuaded by the Kolmsaare link because the aftershocks sit along the structure's mapped trend.

q1.1: The felt account was published: it "went to a newspaper the same week", so it is not something the logbook alone preserves.
q1.2: The run of the station is not in dispute — the logbook "closes in the same year" the official history gives.
q1.3: The recovered crate came another way, "through a museum's accession list", not from a logbook entry.

q2.0: The double-event reading is rejected: "the trace shows one rupture".
q2.1: Correcting the old instruments changes little — "the magnitude barely moves".
q2.2: The location stands as catalogued: "the source sits under the coastal parish" the catalogues name.

q3.0: Survival is nearly complete, and not patchy by ownership: "hardly a sheet is missing" from the years the network changed hands.
q3.2: The early record is not thin — the years before nineteen fifteen are "as thickly covered as any".
q3.3: Attribution was never in doubt, since "each sheet carries its station's stamp".

q4.1: The rival to the north is dismissed on its own ground: "the northern structure fits the uplift no better".
q4.2: A diffuse reading is denied — "these are not scattered shocks in healed crust".
q4.3: It is not an inherited weakness in his account: "the Kolmsaare structure is young", by what the mapping shows.

atv2-b4-p3.transcript: The Vantsi roll — nine metres of notation, and the question everyone asks first: which staging is this? My answer is the plain one. It is the first staging. Look at the ensemble figures: thirty-two dancers crammed into the downstage third, exactly the crowding the opening reviews complained of. The ensemble numbers here are not thinned, they are packed. Nor is this a drill book — the roll follows one evening's order straight through — and the entrances are in the same ink and the same hand as the figures, so nobody redrew them for a later season. What does it actually record? The corps, in detail. Their steps are written out in full, each number carried through to its end. The soloists get a line of description apiece, no more. And the mime scenes are passed over in a phrase, where later notations linger on them. Now the wrapper. There is a customs stamp on it, and three articles have built an itinerary out of that stamp. The stamp dates a crate of linen thread, not the roll's journey; the wrapper is freight paper somebody reused, and the address on it has sent people to the wrong city. Wrapper and roll are of a piece, the same decade, and the stamp is a western port's. Next? We are going to dance it. One suite, with students, in the spring — the performance is the test. The order of the numbers is not in doubt, so the orchestral parts can wait, the rubbed passages were already read under raking light last winter, and the ballroom manuals are somebody else's project.

explanations.q1: She endorses the first-staging claim: the ensemble figures put thirty-two dancers into the downstage third, exactly the crowding the opening reviews complained of.
explanations.q2: The notation is detailed for the corps — their steps written out in full — while each soloist's variation is reduced to a single line of description.
explanations.q3: The next step is to stage one suite with students in the spring, with the performance itself serving as the test of the notation.
explanations.q4: The customs stamp shows the wrapper is reused freight paper, so the address on it has sent earlier researchers to the wrong city.

q1.0: A revival with a reduced corps is exactly what she denies: "the ensemble numbers here are not thinned", they are packed.
q1.1: It is not a drill document — "the roll follows one evening's order" straight through.
q1.3: The entrances are original too, being in "the same ink and the same hand" as the figures.

q2.0: The steps are not left to conventional signs: for the corps they are "written out in full".
q2.2: Coverage is not partial — each number is "carried through to its end".
q2.3: The mime gets much less, not equal space: "the mime scenes are passed over" in a phrase.

q3.1: The ordering question is closed, so "the orchestral parts can wait".
q3.2: That work is done — the rubbed passages were "already read under raking light" last winter.
q3.3: She hands that line off: "the ballroom manuals are somebody else's project".

q4.0: The stamp belongs to the paper's earlier life — it dates a crate of linen thread, "not the roll's journey".
q4.2: There is no gap between them: "wrapper and roll are of a piece", the same decade.
q4.3: The direction is the other one, since "the stamp is a western port's".

atv2-b4-p4.transcript: Sarvela's beetles — eleven thousand pins, and questions the specimens cannot settle. Start with the coastal meadows. The literature says Kepsara's ground beetle vanished around nineteen ten. Rehepapp takes that at face value. Ilves says the older records are misidentified relatives, since the sister species was not split off until the fifties and much of the coastal literature predates the split — a fair worry. But I have been through the trays: the old specimens are there, and they are correctly named. Nor did the beetle shift inland: the drained margins have been swept, and swept well, since the sixties. The post-war sweeping in the meadows themselves amounts to two afternoons. What thins out around nineteen ten is the collecting, not the beetle. The nineteen-oh-four auction catalogue. One copy carries a pencil note naming the buyer, whose heirs gave us the material — that is how the chain closes. Its lot descriptions run to a line each, too thin to match a box against, the prices in it are steep for the day, and the cabinet it lists came to the museum with the rest. The labels. There is no pencil under the ink; one hand wrote the coastal labels and its abbreviations don't vary; the oldest hand is Sarvela's own, from his school years. What the writing shows is a nineteen-thirties re-curation: a good many labels rewritten, the old spellings quietly modernized. Next: not re-pinning, the pins stay where Sarvela put them; not sequencing, we won't cut them; not the traded duplicates, Vaher published that list years ago. The mites that ride on these beetles — nobody has looked.

explanations.q1: The professor rules out re-pinning, sequencing and the duplicate trade, and ends on the mites riding on the beetles as the thing nobody has looked at.
explanations.q2: He treats the disappearance as an artifact of collecting effort: post-war sweeping in those meadows amounts to two afternoons, so what thins out is the collecting, not the beetle.
explanations.q3: The catalogue matters for a pencil note in one copy that names the buyer, whose heirs later gave the material to the museum — it closes the provenance chain.
explanations.q4: The handwriting shows a nineteen-thirties re-curation in which many labels were rewritten and the old spellings quietly modernized.

q1.1: Destructive sampling is refused: "we won't cut them".
q1.3: The duplicate trail is already published — "Vaher published that list years ago".

atv2-b4-p5.transcript: Turvaste — three parish volumes, and the crisis years at their centre. What the registers show is not a parish dying evenly. The burials fall heavily on households that had arrived within the previous decade, cottagers, hired men, families off the road, while the long-settled farms came through comparatively lightly. Not departure: the town lists show no bulge of arrivals from here in those years. Not two waves either — the burials run in one long swell. And the hamlets and the church village lost at much the same rate. Now, the entries. Halliste built a good deal on the cause column, and Piir on the lists at the back, both worth having: each says the register shapes what we think we see. But the cause column runs right through the crisis, and stillbirths are entered in the main sequence. The entries give a name and a farm, and leave the messenger out. The close reading shows the clerk wrote up several days at a time, so the day-by-day dating everyone quotes is ours, not the parish's. The eighteen-eighties rebinding. The margins came through it uncut, no bill for the work has been found, and the covers went back on plain. What did happen is that a few leaves from the parish upriver were bound in by mistake, and nobody caught it until the nineteen thirties. Next? Not the rent rolls, Turvaste's burned in the eighteen forties. Not the neighbours, whose registers are in poor shape. Grain prices are already in the appendix of my first article. I want the slow method: reconstituting a sample of households in full.

explanations.q1: Her central claim is that the crisis fell unevenly by length of settlement — burials concentrated among households arrived within the previous decade, while long-settled farms came through comparatively lightly.
explanations.q2: She ends on the slow method she has defended before: reconstituting a sample of households in full.
explanations.q3: The close reading shows the clerk wrote up several days at a time, so the day-by-day dating everyone quotes is the historians' rather than the parish's.
explanations.q4: The rebinding matters because a few leaves from the parish upriver were bound in by mistake, and nobody caught it until the nineteen thirties.

q1.0: Out-migration is excluded: the town lists show "no bulge of arrivals" from Turvaste in those years.
q1.2: There is no second wave — "the burials run in one long swell".
q1.3: Geography does not divide the losses: hamlets and church village lost "at much the same rate".

q2.1: The neighbouring parishes are not usable, being registers that "are in poor shape".
q2.3: The price work is done and published, "already in the appendix" of her first article.

atv2-b4-p6.transcript:
Kuivalinn hall came down in nineteen sixty-one. What survives is Rebasmaa's notebooks, eleven recordings, and Nommiste's drawings. Rebasmaa measured with pistol shots fired from the stage, logged position by position across two evenings. He had asked the mill to send workers in to fill the seats; the mill declined, so the hall stood empty for both sittings. What he entered are the single readings themselves, not averages; no cards stand behind them. The hall was renovated in fifty-four and he did not go back, so that book holds one campaign, not two.

Was the sound as fine as its reputation? I think so: a modern designer would still envy the measured values. The memoirists came late and added little. The resident orchestra was a middling band that toured to no acclaim. And these figures are not the long reverberation that period taste supposedly prized - they are short and defined.

Now the recordings. Cleaned digitally, they can anchor a computed model of the room, which no drawing on its own could support. The players were shifted between takes with no note kept, so the discs will not fix anybody's placement, and the room's contribution sits well above the surface noise once cleaned. The studio discs are a different decade and a different orchestra.

Next, then. Rebuilding a length of that wall at full scale was costed and is beyond us; the museum will mount its exhibition without our help; the local press we have read through already. Nommiste's smaller hall at Harmavere still stands, and we will measure it as our stand-in.

explanations.q1: The professor says Rebasmaa “measured with pistol shots fired from the stage, logged position by position across two evenings” — that is what the notebooks record about the method.
explanations.q2: She credits the reputation and grounds it in the numbers - a modern designer would still envy the measured values.
explanations.q3: Her central point about the discs is that, cleaned digitally, they can anchor a computed model of the room that no drawing on its own could support.
explanations.q4: The other options are closed off in turn, and the plan she states is to measure Nommiste's surviving smaller hall at Harmavere as a stand-in for the lost one.

q1.2: There is no second campaign in the book — after the renovation he did not go back, so "that book holds one campaign, not two".
q1.3: What is written in is "the single readings themselves, not averages", and no cards stand behind them.

q2.1: The posthumous memoir story is set aside: "The memoirists came late and added little".
q2.2: The orchestra cannot carry the fame — it was "a middling band that toured to no acclaim".
q2.3: The values are "not the long reverberation that period taste supposedly prized"; they are short and defined.

q3.2: The room is not buried under the surface noise — its contribution "sits well above the surface noise once cleaned".

q4.2: The press search is finished, not planned: "the local press we have read through already".

atv2-b4-p7.transcript:
The Aravik lot - two hundred pieces, bought in nineteen twelve, and a century of muddle since. That muddle has a cause: Pellamaa's day-book. His running numbers show the lot was renumbered at the sale itself, and that explains the two conflicting catalogue sequences. The book is not barren otherwise. It records a partner, but he is named on the first page, and his papers came to us in nineteen forty. Its months run at an even pace, with no slow seasons to read; and the permit-suspension years are, oddly, the book's busiest.

Fibre work next. The lot's ancient repairs use strips cut from a discarded letter, and that letter is now the oldest text we hold. The sheets are of one manufacture throughout. The literary pieces are on fresh sheets, not reused accounts. Ilmsalu checked the register against the trays last spring, expecting parchments booked as papyrus - the register and the trays agree.

So where did the lot come from? Pellamaa built it from several finds, matching pieces by look to make a salable whole. There is no shared damp stain on these sheets. Nor did it come out of a rubbish mound; there is no town soil. Ilmsalu reads the frame marks as an older collection redispersed, a fair reading - but those marks are our own mounting shop's.

Next, the editors go to Norvalt, which bought from the same source in the same season, and try for joins. The documentary texts wait; the cartonnage stays where it is; the concordance of hands is a student's job for later.

explanations.q1: Pellamaa's day-book is brought up because its running numbers show the lot was renumbered at the sale itself, which is why two conflicting catalogue sequences have been in circulation.
explanations.q2: The fibre work found that the lot's ancient repairs use strips cut from a discarded letter, and that letter is now the oldest text in the collection.
explanations.q3: The stated next move is a trip to Norvalt, which bought from the same source in the same season, to try for joins.
explanations.q4: The professor's central claim is that Pellamaa built the lot from several finds, matching pieces by look to make a salable whole.

q1.3: The permit years are not blank in it; they "are, oddly, the book's busiest".

atv2-b4-p8.transcript:
Soorna is a small brown lake with a deep archive: Virkland's notebooks from the eighteen nineties, the fishermen's association minute-books, and our series since eighty-eight.

The minute-books first: they settle a dating problem. The association paid Virkland's boatman by the day, and the payments are dated, fixing the seasons his notebooks leave vague. Their other contents are thin. The net-fouling complaints are undated grumbles; the argument about the springs names no location, being a quarrel over payment; and the catch was weighed at the landing for two years before the practice lapsed.

Virkland's transparency readings against ours. They scatter too widely to carry a trend - to his credit the notebooks say why, listing wind and cloud for each cast. The scatter is not a steady offset. His figures run deeper on some days and shallower on others, in the bays and on the open water alike, and matching him week for week does not tighten the cloud.

Kivrand argues the darkening began centuries before the first surveys. I reject that. Those proxies move whenever a lake's level shifts, whatever colour the water is - and Soorna's level has shifted. So I am not dating the onset a little later than Kivrand does, I am not pushing it further back on the pollen and charcoal, and I am not calling the darkening periodic either.

Back on the water: the outflow gauge is Tammiste's project; the neighbouring lakes were sampled in ninety-six and written up; the landowners have asked to be kept off the boats. Our first job is Virkland's sunken marker buoys, whose positions carry his depth grid.

explanations.q1: The professor lists the other candidate jobs as already handled or refused, then says the first job on returning is Virkland's sunken marker buoys, whose positions carry his depth grid.
explanations.q2: The minute-books matter because the association paid Virkland's boatman by the day and the payments are dated, which fixes the survey seasons his notebooks leave vague.
explanations.q3: He rejects Kivrand's early-onset argument on the ground that those proxies move whenever a lake's level shifts, whatever colour the water is.
explanations.q4: The comparison shows Virkland's readings scatter too widely to carry a trend, though his notebooks record wind and cloud for each cast and so explain the scatter.

atv2-b4-p9.transcript:
Kaldevere's garden, laid out in the seventeen nineties, and the question that comes first: was it Nurmsaar's? The design is his; the hand shows in the sweep of the approach. But I doubt he came. The plans travelled by post, and were adapted on site by whoever held the spade. The estate books enter no payment for a visit; his pupil's planting lists, which Harm compares with the beds, are a poor match; and the family were naming Nurmsaar in their own letters within two years of the digging, not a generation after.

Now the drawings against the ground. Harm reads the showpiece drawing as a tidied presentation piece, symmetrical on paper and loose in the soil, and I would believe that elsewhere. Here the bed edges we dug out in ninety-four sit where the drawing puts them, foot for foot, through the first campaign. Then it was set aside within a decade, as taste turned. The same sheet governs the park and the walled ground alike, and there is no rival drawing to braid it with.

The nursery invoices. Substitutions run right through them: Parnaste sent hardier kinds than the ones ordered. They date the water garden where the guidebooks do; they are made out to the steward; and the estate's own nursery supplied little beyond seed.

Tiidema's letter-book, last. It is a thin thing - a handful of letters, there are no blotting pages bound in, and his famous quarrel is not in it. What it does is show him at Kaldevere from boyhood, against the story that he was fetched from abroad.

explanations.q1: She keeps the design as Nurmsaar's — the hand shows in the sweep of the approach — but doubts he came: the plans travelled by post and were adapted on site by whoever held the spade.
explanations.q2: Her central claim is that the main drawing guided the first campaign closely, with the dug bed edges sitting where it puts them, and that it was then set aside within a decade as taste turned.
explanations.q3: The invoices show substitutions running right through them, with Parnaste sending hardier kinds than the ones ordered.
explanations.q4: The letter-book is raised because it shows Tiidema at Kaldevere from boyhood, against the story that he was fetched from abroad.
